questions.stem: A 23 year old nursery nurse who never had MMR has had 4 days of fever, a hacking cough, a runny nose and sore red eyes. Yesterday a red blotchy rash began at her hairline and is spreading down to her trunk. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. There are small white spots on the buccal mucosa opposite her molars.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Cough, coryza and conjunctivitis followed by a rash spreading from the hairline, with Koplik spots, in an unvaccinated adult is measles. It is urgently notifiable, so the GP phones the health protection team the same day.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: small white spots on the buccal mucosa
steps.x: Fever, rash and feeling unwell in an unvaccinated person is the exam's measles cue; Koplik spots clinch it.

elim: That rash is non-blanching purpura with shock, not a maculopapular rash after a coryzal prodrome.
Milder illness with a pink rash and post-auricular nodes; no Koplik spots or marked conjunctivitis.
Sandpaper rash with sore throat and strawberry tongue, not cough, coryza and conjunctivitis.
Itchy vesicles in crops, not a blotchy rash spreading from the hairline.

steps.x: A: Measles. Measles: notify immediately on clinical suspicion.

questions.stem: A 5 year old girl whose parents declined all childhood vaccines has coughed for 3 weeks. She has spells of 20 or more coughs in a row, after which she sometimes vomits, and she gasps noisily as she breathes in at the end of a bout. Between bouts she is well and playing. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Her chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Paroxysmal cough, inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting in an unvaccinated child, well between bouts, is whooping cough (Bordetella pertussis), a notifiable disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: 20 or more coughs in a row
gasps noisily as she breathes in
steps.x: Paroxysms, whoop and post-tussive vomiting, with no vaccines, point to pertussis.

elim: Wheeze and nocturnal cough with response to inhalers; not paroxysms ending in an inspiratory whoop and vomiting.
An infant illness with crackles and wheeze, not paroxysms in a 5 year old.
Barking cough with stridor over a few days, not 3 weeks of paroxysms.
Sudden onset with unilateral signs, not bouts with a whoop and post-tussive vomiting.

steps.x: E: Whooping cough. Whooping cough is notifiable; unvaccinated children and young infants are most at risk.

questions.stem: A 9 month old boy has been feverish and irritable for 8 hours and now will not feed. His hands and feet are cold and his skin is mottled. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 188 bpm, BP 70/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 50 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. Capillary refill time is 5 seconds. There are purple spots on his legs that do not fade when a glass is pressed on them.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A febrile, shocked infant with a non-blanching purpuric rash has meningococcal septicaemia (Neisseria meningitidis) until proven otherwise. It is urgently notifiable.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: cold and his skin is mottled
do not fade when a glass is pressed
steps.x: Fever plus non-blanching rash plus shock is meningococcal septicaemia.

elim: A well child with palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs, not a shocked febrile infant.
Well child with bruising after a viral illness; no fever or shock.
Maculopapular blanching rash after a coryzal prodrome.
May cause fever in infants but not a non-blanching rash with shock.

steps.x: D: Meningococcal septicaemia. Treat at once and notify the health protection team immediately.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man is brought in by his wife with 1 day of fever, severe headache and increasing confusion. He winces when the curtains are opened. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. There is marked neck stiffness and Kernig's sign is positive. There is no rash.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness and confusion in an older man, with turbid neutrophilic CSF and low glucose, is acute bacterial meningitis, which is notifiable.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: fever, severe headache and increasing confusion
winces when the curtains are opened
steps.x: Fever, meningism and neutrophilic CSF with low glucose = bacterial meningitis.

elim: Behavioural change and seizures with less meningism; CSF is lymphocytic.
Not febrile with meningism and confusion.
Thunderclap onset; fever is not the leading feature.
Milder illness in younger adults; CSF is lymphocytic with normal glucose.

steps.x: A: Acute bacterial meningitis. Acute meningitis is notifiable: notify on suspicion, before culture returns.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has 6 days of tiredness, nausea and aching under his right ribs, and since yesterday his eyes have turned yellow and his urine is dark. He returned from a month backpacking in India 4 weeks ago. He drinks 6 units of alcohol a week and takes no medicines.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A prodrome then jaundice with ALT in the thousands after travel to India is acute infective (viral) hepatitis, probably hepatitis A, which is notifiable.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Travel, prodrome, jaundice and ALT over 1000 = acute viral hepatitis.

elim: Needs heavy, prolonged drinking and the AST usually exceeds the ALT with transaminases in the hundreds.
Episodic pain without a transaminase rise in the thousands.
He takes no medicines.
Isolated mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normal ALT.

steps.x: A: Acute infective hepatitis. Acute infective hepatitis is on the notifiable list.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman who is homeless has had a cough for 10 weeks with night sweats and 6 kg weight loss. She has coughed up streaks of blood twice. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 116/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. A chest X-ray shows right upper zone shadowing with a cavity (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Right upper zone shadowing with cavitation: post-primary TB.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chronic cough, haemoptysis, night sweats and weight loss with an upper zone cavity in a homeless woman is pulmonary TB. It is routinely notifiable (within 3 days) and treatment lasts about 6 months.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: night sweats and 6 kg weight loss
right upper zone shadowing with a cavity
steps.x: Weeks of cough, sweats and weight loss with an apical cavity = TB.

elim: Daily copious purulent sputum over years, not weeks of sweats and weight loss with an apical cavity.
A short illness, not 10 weeks of systemic symptoms.
Swinging fever with foul sputum after aspiration; the setting and course favour TB.
Bilateral hilar nodes, not an apical cavity with haemoptysis.

steps.x: D: Pulmonary tuberculosis. TB is notifiable; active disease needs about 6 months of treatment.

questions.stem: A 19 year old student has 3 days of mild fever, aching knees and a faint pink rash that started on her face and spread to her trunk within a day. She did not have her second MMR dose. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 114/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. There are tender nodes behind her ears and at the back of her neck. She has no cough or conjunctivitis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A mild illness with a pink rash spreading from the face, post-auricular and suboccipital nodes and arthralgia in a partly vaccinated young woman is rubella, a notifiable rash illness.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Mild illness, pink rash, post-auricular nodes and arthralgia = rubella.

elim: Slapped cheek appearance then a lacy limb rash, not post-auricular nodes.
Sore throat, exudative tonsillitis and anterior cervical nodes.
Severe prodrome with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, which she does not have.
Sore throat and sandpaper rash in a child.

steps.x: D: Rubella. Rubella sits with measles in the rash group of notifiable diseases.

questions.stem: An 8 year old boy with measles diagnosed 6 days ago was improving, but today he became drowsy and had a generalised seizure lasting 4 minutes. His mother says he has been talking nonsense. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 120 bpm, BP 100/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. His GCS is 11. There is no neck stiffness and the fading rash is still visible on his trunk.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Drowsiness, confusion and seizures days after measles rash is acute measles encephalitis. Pneumonia and encephalitis are why measles is taken so seriously.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely complication?
New confusion and seizures during measles = encephalitis.

elim: Occurs at 6 months to 6 years with rapid recovery, not persisting confusion in an 8 year old.
Would cause breathlessness and hypoxia, not seizures and reduced GCS.
Ear pain and fever; does not lower the GCS.
Appears years after measles, not within days.

steps.x: B: Measles encephalitis. Measles can cause pneumonia and encephalitis.

questions.stem: A 35 year old aid worker flies home from a refugee camp and develops profuse painless watery diarrhoea that looks like rice water, passing more than 15 litres in a day. She is very thirsty and has leg cramps. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Stool microscopy shows darting comma-shaped Gram-negative rods.
questions.q: Which best describes the notification category of this condition?
questions.e: Rice-water stools with comma-shaped rods after a refugee camp is cholera: a GI notifiable disease that must be reported immediately, alongside meningococcal meningitis, measles and rabies.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best describes the notification category of this condition?
Rice-water diarrhoea and comma-shaped rods = cholera, a GI disease on the urgent list.

elim: Cholera is spread by the faecal-oral route, and it is notified immediately.
Cholera is on the urgent list, not the 3-day list.
Cholera is a GI infection.
Cholera is notifiable.

steps.x: C: Gastrointestinal; urgently notifiable. Cholera: GI type, urgently notifiable.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man who injects heroin attends a drug service with 2 weeks of tiredness and yellow eyes. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. He is jaundiced with a tender liver edge. Investigations show hepatitis B surface antigen positive and IgM anti-HBc positive.
questions.q: Which best describes the notification category of this condition?
questions.e: HBsAg with IgM anti-HBc in a person who injects drugs is acute hepatitis B: a blood-borne notifiable disease reported routinely within 3 days.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best describes the notification category of this condition?
HBsAg plus IgM anti-HBc = acute hepatitis B, blood-borne.

elim: Hepatitis B is notified routinely, not by immediate telephone call.
Hepatitis B is spread by blood and body fluids, not faecal-oral.
HIV is not notifiable but hepatitis B is.
That describes measles.

steps.x: A: Blood-borne; routinely notifiable within 3 days. Hepatitis B: blood-borne, routine, within 3 days.

questions.stem: A GP partner audits the practice's notifications for the month. The new diagnoses were secondary syphilis in a 34 year old man, pulmonary TB in a 60 year old woman, measles in a 2 year old, whooping cough in a 4 month old and acute hepatitis B in a 29 year old.
questions.q: Which diagnosis does not need to be notified?
questions.e: Syphilis, like HIV and herpes simplex, is monitored through sexual health surveillance but is not legally notifiable by the clinician. The other four must be reported.

steps.x: The question asks: Which diagnosis does not need to be notified?
Know the 'not notifiable' list: HIV, syphilis, herpes simplex, ophthalmia neonatorum.

elim: Routinely notifiable, within 3 days.
Urgently notifiable, the same day.
Routinely notifiable, within 3 days.
Notifiable, especially important in young infants.

steps.x: D: Secondary syphilis. Syphilis is not legally notifiable.

questions.stem: A sexual health clinic doctor reviews today's diagnoses before writing to the health protection team: primary genital herpes simplex in a 22 year old woman, Campylobacter food poisoning in a 40 year old chef, rubella in a 17 year old, acute meningitis in a 19 year old and TB lymphadenitis in a 33 year old.
questions.q: Which diagnosis does not need to be notified?
questions.e: Herpes simplex is not legally notifiable. Food poisoning, rubella, meningitis and TB (pulmonary or extrapulmonary) are.

steps.x: The question asks: Which diagnosis does not need to be notified?
Herpes simplex sits with HIV and syphilis on the not-notifiable list.

elim: Notifiable (neurological), and urgently so if meningococcal.
Food poisoning is routinely notifiable within 3 days.
A notifiable rash illness.
TB of any site is notifiable.

steps.x: C: Genital herpes simplex. Herpes simplex is not notifiable.

questions.stem: Thirty-two guests at a wedding develop vomiting, cramping abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea 4 to 6 hours after the reception meal. Several have fever. Most improve within 2 days with oral fluids. Stool samples from three guests grow Salmonella enteritidis, and the caterer used raw egg in a mayonnaise.
questions.q: Under which type of notifiable disease is this outbreak classified?
questions.e: A food-borne outbreak of vomiting and diarrhoea is food poisoning, a gastrointestinal notifiable disease (with cholera). It is routinely notifiable within 3 days.

steps.x: The question asks: Under which type of notifiable disease is this outbreak classified?

clues: vomiting, cramping abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea
steps.x: A shared meal and GI symptoms = food poisoning, the GI group.

elim: Examples are hepatitis B.
Examples are meningitis.
Examples are measles and rubella.
Examples are TB; not a food-borne outbreak.

steps.x: B: Gastrointestinal. Food poisoning is a GI notifiable disease, notified within 3 days.

questions.stem: A 3 year old unvaccinated boy has 4 days of fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis and a maculopapular rash spreading from behind his ears. The GP is confident it is measles. His mother asks whether the doctor must wait for a blood test before 'officially' reporting it.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate basis for notifying this case?
o: Clinical diagnosis now, with formal notification
Measles IgG on a blood sample
Measles IgM result from the reference laboratory
Review once the rash has fully evolved
questions.e: For notifiable diseases the 'gold standard' is a clinical diagnosis plus formal notification. The doctor notifies on clinical suspicion and does not wait for laboratory confirmation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate basis for notifying this case?

clues: The GP is confident it is measles
steps.x: Notification rests on clinical suspicion, not on a lab result.

elim: IgG shows past infection or vaccination, and notification does not wait for it.
Lab confirmation follows notification; it is not needed first.
Useful to confirm afterwards, but notification is on suspicion.
Delay loses the window to protect contacts.

steps.x: A: Clinical diagnosis now, with formal notification. Clinical diagnosis plus formal notification; never wait for the lab.

questions.stem: A 6 week old girl is admitted with 10 days of coughing bouts that end with her going blue and then gasping. Her mother did not have the pertussis vaccine in pregnancy. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 160 bpm, BP 80/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 48 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. The admitting doctor has already notified the health protection team on clinical suspicion.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Nasopharyngeal swab for Bordetella pertussis PCR
questions.e: After notification, whooping cough is confirmed by PCR (or culture) on a nasopharyngeal swab, best within 2 to 3 weeks of onset. Serology is used later.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

clues: coughing bouts that end with her going blue
did not have the pertussis vaccine
steps.x: Notify first, then confirm: PCR on a pernasal swab for pertussis.

elim: Bordetella pertussis does not cause bacteraemia.
Usually normal or non-specific; does not identify the organism.
May show lymphocytosis but is not confirmatory.
An infant cannot produce sputum; a pernasal swab is used.

steps.x: D: Nasopharyngeal swab for Bordetella pertussis PCR. Confirmatory tests after notification: PCR, culture, serology.

questions.stem: A 24 year old unvaccinated man is seen in the emergency department with 5 days of fever, cough and red eyes and a confluent rash spreading from his face. The registrar telephones the health protection team and isolates him in a side room.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Measles PCR on a throat or oral fluid swab
questions.e: Once notified, measles is confirmed with PCR on a throat swab or oral fluid (or IgM serology). The test does not delay notification.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

clues: confluent rash spreading from his face
steps.x: Viral rash illness: confirm with PCR or serology after notifying.

elim: Measles is a virus; blood cultures are for bacteria.
Only if pneumonia is suspected; it does not confirm measles.
No meningism; not a confirmatory test for measles.
Tests for EBV, not measles.

steps.x: D: Measles PCR on a throat or oral fluid swab. Measles: PCR or IgM serology confirms after notification.

questions.stem: A 52 year old care home cook has 2 days of bloody diarrhoea, cramping abdominal pain and fever after eating undercooked chicken at a barbecue. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Her GP suspects food poisoning and notifies the health protection team because of her job.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause?
questions.e: Food poisoning is confirmed by stool culture and PCR (Campylobacter is likely after undercooked chicken). Her work in food handling makes notification and confirmation important.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause?
GI notifiable disease: confirm with stool microbiology.

elim: Only for suspected toxic megacolon; does not identify an organism.
Not a first test in acute infective diarrhoea.
A marker of inflammation, not of the organism.
For pancreatitis.

steps.x: E: Stool culture and PCR. Stool culture/PCR confirms food poisoning.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man has 3 weeks of malaise and jaundice. He had unprotected sex with several partners while travelling in South-East Asia 3 months ago. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 120/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. His ALT is 1650 U/L. The doctor suspects acute viral hepatitis and notifies the health protection team.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm hepatitis B?
o: Hepatitis B serology (HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc)
questions.e: Serology confirms hepatitis B after notification: HBsAg shows infection and IgM anti-HBc shows that it is acute.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm hepatitis B?
Blood-borne virus: confirm with serology.

elim: Shows liver texture and bile ducts; cannot identify the virus.
Invasive and not needed to confirm acute infection.
For haemochromatosis.
Confirms conjugated jaundice, not the cause.

steps.x: B: Hepatitis B serology (HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc). Hepatitis B: HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man from Pakistan has had a cough for 8 weeks with night sweats and weight loss. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 124/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. There are crackles at the right apex. The doctor notifies suspected TB and sends three sputum samples for acid-fast bacilli.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional investigation?
questions.e: Alongside confirmatory microbiology, imaging is an additional test where relevant: in suspected pulmonary TB a chest X-ray looks for upper zone shadowing and cavitation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate additional investigation?
Microbiology confirms; imaging adds information.

elim: Only if sputum cannot be obtained.
For pulmonary embolism.
No cardiac features.
Does not help diagnose TB.

steps.x: B: Chest X-ray. Chest X-ray is the additional imaging test in suspected TB.

questions.stem: A GP registrar sees a 2 year old with fever, cough, conjunctivitis and a maculopapular rash and diagnoses measles. Her supervising GP is on leave, the practice manager offers to handle the paperwork, and the microbiology lab will test a swab tomorrow.
questions.q: Who is legally responsible for notifying this case?
o: The GP registrar who made the diagnosis
The supervising GP when back from leave
questions.e: Under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010 the doctor who suspects the disease is legally responsible for notifying, whatever their grade.

steps.x: The question asks: Who is legally responsible for notifying this case?
The suspecting doctor notifies.

elim: Families are not responsible for statutory notification.
Labs report confirmed organisms separately; this does not replace the clinician's duty.
Not a registered medical practitioner.
Responsibility lies with the doctor who suspects the disease, and delay is unacceptable.

steps.x: B: The GP registrar who made the diagnosis. The doctor who suspects a notifiable disease must notify it.

questions.stem: A foundation doctor in the emergency department sees a 60 year old woman with fever, headache, neck stiffness and confusion. He suspects acute bacterial meningitis, takes blood cultures and starts intravenous ceftriaxone. It is his first notifiable disease and he asks his registrar where the notification should go.
questions.q: To which organisation should the notification be sent?
o: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
UK Health Security Agency (local health protection team)
questions.e: Notifications go to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), via the local health protection team, as set out in the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010.

steps.x: The question asks: To which organisation should the notification be sent?
Notifiable disease goes to public health: UKHSA.

elim: Regulates care providers; does not receive notifications.
Regulates doctors.
For adverse drug reactions (Yellow Card).
Commissions services; not the notification route.

steps.x: E: UK Health Security Agency (local health protection team). Submit notifications to UKHSA.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman attending antenatal booking is found to be hepatitis B surface antigen positive. She is well, with normal liver tests, and was born in Nigeria. The midwife refers her and the hospital doctor confirms new hepatitis B infection.
questions.q: Within which timeframe should the doctor notify the health protection team?
o: Only once the baby is born
questions.e: Hepatitis B is routinely notifiable, so the written notification is sent within 3 days. Immediate telephone notification is for urgent diseases.

steps.x: The question asks: Within which timeframe should the doctor notify the health protection team?
Routine list (TB, hepatitis B, food poisoning) = within 3 days.

elim: Reserved for urgent conditions such as meningococcal disease, measles, cholera and rabies.
Hepatitis B is notifiable.
Notification is not delayed.
Too long; routine notification is within 3 days.

steps.x: E: Within 3 days. Routine notifiable disease: notify within 3 days.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man returns from rural India where he was bitten on the hand by a stray dog 6 weeks ago. He had no vaccine. He now has fever, agitation and painful spasms of his throat when offered a drink of water. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 150/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate action regarding notification?
o: No notification as it was acquired abroad
Notify by post at the end of the week
Notify only if the brain biopsy confirms rabies
questions.e: Dog bite abroad then hydrophobia is rabies, one of the urgently notifiable diseases: notify the health protection team immediately by phone, then in writing.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate action regarding notification?

clues: bitten on the hand by a stray dog
painful spasms of his throat when offered a drink
steps.x: Rabies is on the urgent list with meningococcal disease, measles and cholera.

elim: Where it was acquired does not matter.
Too slow for an urgent condition.
Notification never waits for confirmation.
The routine window, not for rabies.

steps.x: C: Notify immediately by telephone. Urgent notifiable disease: notify immediately.

questions.stem: A 3 year old girl is diagnosed with measles and notified. Her 14 month old brother, who has not yet had MMR, shares her bedroom. The health protection team calls the GP the next day, about 36 hours after the brother's first exposure. He is well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management for the brother?
o: Reassure and review if a rash develops
questions.e: Unvaccinated contacts of measles are offered MMR within 72 hours of exposure. This early intervention is one reason measles is notifiable.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management for the brother?

clues: 14 month old brother, who has not yet had MMR
steps.x: Measles contact, unvaccinated, within 72 hours = MMR now.

elim: For varicella or herpes, not measles.
Chemoprophylaxis for meningococcal contacts, not measles.
Misses the chance to prevent infection.
Post-exposure MMR works only within about 72 hours.

steps.x: A: Give MMR vaccine now. Contact prophylaxis: MMR catch-up for measles contacts.

questions.stem: A 20 year old unvaccinated university student is admitted with fever, cough, conjunctivitis and a widespread maculopapular rash. Measles is suspected and has been notified. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 110 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. She is in an open bay on the medical ward next to a woman having chemotherapy.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Give ciprofloxacin to everyone in the bay
Isolate her in a side room with airborne precautions
Keep her in the bay with a surgical mask
questions.e: Infection control is part of managing a notifiable disease: measles is airborne and highly transmissible, so she is isolated in a side room (ideally negative pressure) with airborne precautions.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Highly transmissible airborne infection = isolate.

elim: She is infectious and on a ward with immunosuppressed patients.
Meningococcal prophylaxis; no role in measles.
Measles is airborne; an open bay is not safe.
Measles is viral.

steps.x: C: Isolate her in a side room with airborne precautions. Infection control (isolation) where required.

questions.stem: An 18 year old man has a 6 hour history of fever, vomiting and leg pain and now has a spreading purpuric rash. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 132 bpm, BP 86/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Capillary refill is 4 seconds. Meningococcal septicaemia is suspected.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Lumbar puncture, then antibiotics once the CSF is seen
Oral amoxicillin and notify within 3 days
Wait for blood culture before antibiotics and notification
questions.e: Treat the patient with intravenous antibiotics (ceftriaxone) straight away and notify the health protection team immediately, without waiting for confirmation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
Treat the patient now; notify now.

elim: LP delays treatment and is unsafe in shock.
Oral treatment is inadequate and meningococcal disease is urgently notifiable.
Prophylaxis for contacts, not treatment of the patient.
Never delay antibiotics or notification.

steps.x: A: Intravenous ceftriaxone and notify immediately. Meningococcal disease: IV ceftriaxone, immediate notification.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man is diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary TB and notified. He lives with his partner and their 2 year old son, and works in a busy open-plan office. He has started standard four-drug treatment and asks whether anyone else needs to be involved now that the form has been sent.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate public health step?
o: Give BCG to all office colleagues
Identify and screen his close contacts
No action as he is now on treatment
Start all contacts on full TB treatment
questions.e: After notification, close contacts (household first, especially the young child) are identified and screened for active and latent TB. Contact tracing is part of managing every notifiable disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate public health step?
Notified infection: trace and screen close contacts.

elim: Disproportionate; contacts are assessed instead.
Not how contacts are managed; they are screened first.
Contacts may already be infected.
Only those with active or latent disease on screening are treated.

steps.x: C: Identify and screen his close contacts. Identify and trace close contacts.

questions.stem: A 17 year old girl is admitted at 2 am with fever, headache, neck stiffness and a few petechiae. Ceftriaxone is given. The night registrar says meningococcal PCR will be back in 2 days and plans to 'notify once it is confirmed, so we don't waste public health time'.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice to the registrar?
o: Ask the microbiologist to notify instead
Notify within 3 days of the PCR result
Only notify if a contact becomes unwell
Wait for the PCR result as planned
questions.e: Suspected meningococcal disease is urgently notifiable: notify immediately on clinical suspicion. Waiting for PCR would delay prophylaxis for contacts.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice to the registrar?

clues: fever, headache, neck stiffness and a few petechiae
steps.x: Suspicion, not confirmation, triggers notification.

elim: The suspecting doctor is responsible.
Wrong timeframe and wrong trigger.
Notification is meant to prevent that.
Lab confirmation must not delay notification.

steps.x: B: Notify now on clinical suspicion. Do not wait for lab confirmation.

questions.stem: A 4 day old baby boy has bilateral red, swollen eyelids with a thick purulent discharge. His mother had untreated chlamydia. The paediatric registrar diagnoses ophthalmia neonatorum, sends eye swabs and starts treatment. The foundation doctor asks whether a notification form is needed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate answer?
o: Notify only if gonococcus is grown
Notify within 3 days and inform the GMC
questions.e: Ophthalmia neonatorum has recently been removed from the list of notifiable diseases. The baby still needs treatment and the mother and partner need sexual health follow-up.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate answer?

steps.x: Remember the not-notifiable list: HIV, syphilis, herpes simplex, ophthalmia neonatorum.

steps.x: A: Notification is not legally required. Ophthalmia neonatorum is no longer notifiable.

questions.stem: A 19 year old student is admitted with fever, neck stiffness and a non-blanching rash and is notified as suspected meningococcal disease. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Her CSF Gram stain shows intracellular Gram-negative diplococci.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci with a purpuric rash in a young adult is Neisseria meningitidis, the cause of urgently notifiable meningococcal disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely causative organism?
Gram-negative diplococci + purpura = meningococcus.

elim: Gram-negative coccobacillus, now rare after vaccination.
Gram-positive rod in neonates, the elderly and the immunosuppressed.
Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
Gram-positive diplococci; no purpuric rash usually.

steps.x: C: Neisseria meningitidis. Meningococcal disease is caused by Neisseria meningitidis.

questions.stem: During a teaching session on the acute medical unit, a student asks why doctors must notify suspected meningococcal disease within hours of seeing the patient, rather than waiting until the laboratory confirms the organism by culture or PCR several days later. The patient is already receiving ceftriaxone.
questions.q: Which is the main purpose of notification on clinical suspicion?
o: To allow rapid public health action such as prophylaxis for contacts
To ensure the patient receives free treatment
To protect the doctor from litigation
To speed up the laboratory result
questions.e: Notifiable disease legislation lets public health teams act quickly (contact tracing, prophylaxis, outbreak control) before lab confirmation would otherwise delay action.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the main purpose of notification on clinical suspicion?

Not its purpose.

steps.x: A: To allow rapid public health action such as prophylaxis for contacts. Purpose: rapid intervention before confirmation.

questions.stem: A public health registrar is teaching students on placement at the local health protection team. She explains why some infections, such as measles and meningococcal disease, are placed on the notifiable list while others, such as the common cold and most cases of viral tonsillitis, are not.
questions.q: Which best explains how diseases are chosen for notifiable status?
o: Transmissibility, severity and the value of early intervention
questions.e: Diseases are made notifiable based on transmissibility, severity and whether early action helps (for example PEP for meningococcal contacts or MMR catch-up for measles contacts).

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains how diseases are chosen for notifiable status?
Spread, severity and a useful intervention decide the list.

elim: Many notifiable diseases are rarely fatal (food poisoning).
Many are managed at home.
Food poisoning has no vaccine; HIV is not notifiable.
Measles, rabies and hepatitis are viral.

steps.x: E: Transmissibility, severity and the value of early intervention. Transmissibility, severity, value of early intervention.

questions.stem: A medical student notices that a ward doctor phoned the health protection team the same day about a patient with suspected meningococcal meningitis, but sent a written form two days after diagnosing smear-positive pulmonary TB in another patient on the same ward. Both diagnoses were made on clinical grounds.
questions.q: Which best explains why TB can be notified within 3 days?
o: TB has a lower immediate outbreak risk than meningococcal disease
TB is less severe than meningococcal disease
TB is not infectious once diagnosed
TB needs culture confirmation before notification
questions.e: Meningococcal disease has a short incubation and high transmissibility, so contacts need prophylaxis within hours. TB has a lower immediate outbreak risk, so a 3-day window is allowed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains why TB can be notified within 3 days?

steps.x: Short incubation and fast spread = immediate; lower immediate risk = 3 days.

elim: TB can be fatal; the window reflects outbreak risk and incubation.

steps.x: A: TB has a lower immediate outbreak risk than meningococcal disease. Timeframe follows outbreak risk.

questions.stem: The household contacts of a 15 year old with meningococcal meningitis are given ciprofloxacin by the health protection team on the evening of the day she was admitted. A student on placement asks why the notification had to be made so fast, by telephone, rather than by written form later in the week.
questions.q: Which feature of meningococcal disease best explains the need for immediate notification?
o: It can only be diagnosed clinically
It has a long incubation period
It is resistant to most antibiotics
It mainly spreads by contaminated food
Short incubation with secondary cases occurring within days
questions.e: Meningococcal disease has a short incubation and high transmissibility, so secondary cases can occur within days. Immediate notification allows prompt chemoprophylaxis of contacts.

steps.x: The question asks: Which feature of meningococcal disease best explains the need for immediate notification?

steps.x: Short incubation + spread + effective prophylaxis = immediate notification.
